svg.title: SDLC with a copilot vs DevFlow
svg.desc: Side-by-side comparison of a conventional lifecycle with an AI coding assistant and the DevFlow loop: stages, the DevFlow artifact chain, which gates are written rules versus enforced, trade-offs, when to use each, and how a production incident opens the next cycle. Sources: the repo README.md and docs/; claim-by-claim source mapping in PR #72.
svg.text: SDLC with a copilot vs DevFlow
Same goal: reviewed, shipped code. A different answer to where the context lives.
Your current lifecycle, with an AI assistant in the IDE.
Familiar stages and tools; the assistant helps where you invoke it.

g.text: with a copilot in the IDE

svg.text: No process change: it fits the tools and rituals
Context lives in people, tickets and handoffs;
each AI session starts from what it is given.
A spec-driven loop for Claude Code and Codex.
Stages write files in .planning/ that later stages read.
The work leaves a trail of files in git, so any
Upfront discipline: requirements, roadmap and plans
before code. /flow-quick and the lite tier trim it.
Plain files in git, versioned with the code. The agent reads .planning/STATE.md first, then follows the chain, so a cold session loses nothing.
/flow-quick small fix: atomic commit and a log line, no phase ceremony
/flow-audit read-only: do the artifacts agree? --drift: with the code?
Most gates are written rules the skills follow. Only some are enforced by the host or by an opt-in hook.
Open a PR, merge, push tags
Written human gates: the skill stops with FLOW: GATE and waits, even under /goal or /loop.
A human merges. Whether GitHub enforces that is your repo's branch protection, not DevFlow.
A human walks the UAT test plan. The skill must not record results or write SIGNOFF.md on its own.
/flow-release is explicit-only (Claude Code won't let the model start it). It aborts unless SIGNOFF.md's sha
matches HEAD, then asks for an explicit yes before deploying.
Opt-in: installs five Claude Code PreToolUse guards (base branch, secret scan, protected paths, dependencies,
destructive git). A backstop to the written rules, not a sandbox: fails open on infra errors, misses wrapper scripts.
Each gate answer goes to DECISIONS.md: what was asked, what the human said, who, and the SHA.
None: keep your tools and rituals
Real: requirements, roadmap, plans, checks and gates
.planning/ files in git, next to the code
Read STATE.md; it names the next command
Human PR review, plus whatever tools you run
Lens subagents; --adversarial adds a peer provider + ledger
Found in review or a retro
/flow-audit, read-only; --drift checks code and git history
/flow-quick: atomic commit, logged, no phase ceremony
Higher: DevFlow's main cost (the lite tier trims it)
Keep SDLC with a copilot when
your process already works, changes are small, and the
people reviewing them hold the context.
agents do multi-step work across sessions, and someone later
has to trace a change from requirement through plan and
/flow-debug --incident (investigate now) or /flow-todo --incident (later) takes pasted alert text, ServiceMonitor output, or an App Insights / incident link.
Traced to the release deployed then (SHA, UAT sign-off, PRs) from release-* tags, PIPELINE.md and SIGNOFF.md. Attribution can be ambiguous or unknown.
Deployed at the time is not the cause. Links are never fetched; pasted text is data, never run. No listener or daemon; human gates unchanged.
Sources: repo README.md and docs/ · source mapping in PR #72 · DevFlow 0.46.0
